newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan c.bank, in trial, sets expanded NCD issue.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan c.bank, in trial, sets expanded NCD issue.

text.p: Taiwan's central bank, in an innovation, said it would launch a further issue of negotiable certificates of deposit on Friday at the 6.442 percent yield set through a morning NCD issue of T$3 billion.
The total value of 14-day NCDs to be issued in the non-bidding afternoon tranche would be determined by market demand, a central bank official said.
Applications for the issue would close at 14.30 local time (0630 GMT), the official said.
The official declined to say whether the central bank had any internal limit on the size of the issue.
"You submit your application; we'll decide the amount," he said without further explanation.
The central has said in recent days that it planned to experiment with new forms of NCD issuance, including such same-day expanded issues.
The central bank official declined to say why the bank chose this day to try out the new method.

The bank maintains that its NCD issuance is merely a tool for fine-tuning liquidity on a day-to-day basis, denying that it is linked directly to Taiwan's feverish stock market -- which has been siphoning capital from the money market.

Analysts say they believe the stock market has been a key factor behind the central bank's NCD strategy, as NCD issuance has tended to accelerate at times of extremely high stock market turnover or rapid rises in the stock index.
Friday was no exception. The central bank arranged the initial T$3 billion NCD issue on the heels of a 2.68 percent stock index rise on Thursday.
Even as the Friday morning issue was executed, the index was surging a further 1.83 percent on extremely high turnover of T$208 billion -- far above Thursday's subdued T$151 billion.
In the morning NCD issue, the average yield was 6.442 percent, the central bank said.
The range of the bids was between 6.351 and 6.500 percent.

Central bank chief Sheu Yuan-dong said last week the bank would not adjust monetary policy merely to cool Taiwan's red-hot stock market, saying such moves were no "cure all" in the face of concerns of overheating.
